otan2 operator math 
The atan2 function (short for 2-argument arctangent) is a mathematical operator that 
calculates the angle between the positive x-axis and a point \((x, y)\) in a 2D Euclidean 
plane. 
Unlike the standard single-argument arctangent (\(\tan ^{-1}\) or \(\text{atan}\)), atan2 
tracks the specific quadrant of the coordinate system. This allows it to return a 
precise angle across the full range of a circle. 
 
      The Core Problem atan2 Solves 
If you use the standard trigonometry formula \(\theta = \tan^{-1}(y/x)\), you run into two 
major issues: 
1. Information Loss (Sign Stripping): The division \(y/x\) loses the independent 
signs of the numbers. For example, \(\frac{3}{3} = 1\) (Quadrant I) and \(\frac{-3}{-
3} = 1\) (Quadrant III) yield the exact same fraction. A standard \(\tan^{-1}(1)\) will 
only ever give you \(45^{\circ }\), missing the fact that the second point is actually 
at \(225^{\circ }\). 
2. Division by Zero: If \(x = 0\) (a point resting directly on the vertical y-axis), 
computing \(y/x\) forces an undefined division by zero error. 
atan2(y, x) accepts both variables separately to completely bypass these issues. 
 
    How it Works (Mathematical Definition) 
The operator returns a value in radians, normally bounded between \(-\pi \) and \(\pi \) 
(or \(-180^{\circ }\) to \(180^{\circ }\)): 
\(\text{atan2}(y,x)=\begin{cases}\tan ^{-1}(\frac{y}{x})&\text{if\ }x>0\\ \tan ^{-
1}(\frac{y}{x})+\pi &\text{if\ }x<0\text{\ and\ }y\ge 0\\ \tan ^{-1}(\frac{y}{x})-\pi &\text{if\ 
}x<0\text{\ and\ }y<0\\ +\frac{\pi }{2}&\text{if\ }x=0\text{\ and\ }y>0\\ -\frac{\pi 
}{2}&\text{if\ }x=0\text{\ and\ }y<0\\ \text{undefined}&\text{if\ }x=0\text{\ and\ 
}y=0\end{cases}\)

    Coding Gotcha: Parameter Order 
Be very careful when typing this into code. Most modern programming languages (like 
Python, C++, Java, and JavaScript) structure the function argument with the vertical 
axis first: 
atan2(y, x) 
However, certain platforms—notably Microsoft Excel and some tracking/mapping 
software—switch the inputs to: 
ATAN2(x, y)

If we were to define an atan2 operator specifically for log-polar encoded data, it 
would behave as a decoding and quadrant-correcting projection operator. 
In standard Cartesian math, atan2(y, x) takes a point (x, y) and extracts its angle θ while 
handling signs and avoiding division by zero. If a point is already log-polar encoded, it 
exists as a coordinate pair (ρ, θ), where \(\rho = \ln(r) = \ln(\sqrt{x^2 + y^2})\). [1]

An atan2 operator built natively for this log-polar space would act differently depending 
on whether you are extracting data from it or processing shifts within it. 
 
      Scenario 1: The "Direct Projection" Operator 
If you feed a log-polar coordinate (ρ, θ) into a log-polar native atan2 operator, the 
operation is mathematically trivial but structurally crucial. 
\(\text{atan2}_{\text{log-polar}}(\rho ,\theta )=\theta \mathinner{\;\left(\mod \,2\pi 
\right)}\) 
• What it does: It completely ignores the log-radial component ρ and directly 
strips out the phase angle θ. 
• The "Quadrant" Fix: Because log-polar space wraps around modularly (moving 
2π brings you back to the same spot), this operator would act as a phase-
unwrapping wrapper. It forces any unbounded or accumulated angular value to 
lock strictly back into the primary range (like \([-\pi, \pi]\) or \([0, 2\pi)\)). [1] 
 
    Scenario 2: The "Vector Difference" Operator (Image Registration) 
In computer vision and image processing, the log-polar transform is famous for Image 
Registration. In Cartesian space, scaling and rotating an image are complex operations. 
But in a log-polar grid, rotation becomes a vertical shift (Δθ) and scaling becomes a 
horizontal shift (Δρ). [1] 
If you were defining an atan2 operator to find the angular offset between two log-polar 
encoded feature vectors A(ρ₁, θ₁) and B(ρ₂, θ₂), the operator would be defined as: 
\(\text{atan2}_{\text{diff}}(A,B)=(\theta _{2}-\theta _{1})\mathinner{\;\left(\mod \,2\pi 
\right)}\) 
Why this is incredibly powerful: 
1. Total Scale Invariance: Because it looks only at the angular components, it can 
calculate the exact rotation between two objects even if one object is 10× larger 
or smaller than the other (ρ₁ ≠ ρ₂). 
2. Singularity Elimination at the Origin: Standard atan2(y, x) completely breaks 
down at the origin (0,0) because the angle is undefined. In log-polar encoding, 
the origin maps to ρ = -∞. A log-polar atan2 operator completely avoids this 
numerical singularity by operating in a space where the origin has effectively 
been pushed out to infinity. [1]
